top.line: One bridge closure, kept as a graph, serves everyone
top.para: A simulation of Markus Franz's bridge example on a story vault: the council said one week, the bridge opened after forty-six days. Three readers used the same claims differently and decided better, institutions and a routing agent bought from the graph, and £2,707 flowed back to the reporter, paper and resident contributors. All fictional.

s0.line: The journalism is getting the reopening date right
s0.para: The council promised a week. The reporter found the three-week, £186,000 contract, heard the same from anonymous workers and got five to seven weeks from an independent engineer. After a second defect, the bridge reopened on 4 December, day forty-six. Each correction supersedes the last claim, so the graph keeps what was believed when.

s1.line: Newsworthy on five days, needed on fifty-seven
s1.para: The paper leads with the bridge on five days, but readers need its current state on fifty-seven, and thirteen days bring real changes worth an alert. That gap between news cycle and need is where money is left on the table. An article is written once; a maintained claim is a service.

s2.line: The same claims served three readers' own graphs differently
s2.para: Hannah booked the after-school club early and walked the footbridge, paying £2.28. Dev planned on six weeks, cut stock and claimed relief, saving £640 of stock and receiving £1,200, for £5.76. Marco clustered jobs and crossed after ten, saving nine hours for 54p. Each reader's graph stays on their device.

s3.line: Without the tracker, each reader decides worse
s3.para: In the counterfactual Hannah is late three days and finds the club full, Dev orders for normal trade three times and applies late, and Marco crosses at peak. The sources are the council's "within a week", page forty-one of a cabinet report, a Facebook rumour and two days of television. Nobody is accountable.

s4.line: Institutions and agents buy the same local graph
s4.para: A county highways team, a fund analyst and a national desk license the evidence. A delivery firm's routing agent planning 140 vans asks the newsroom instead of searching: over 2,392 questions, about $54 instead of $377 in tokens, and right from the 15th rather than wrong for a week. Token prices are illustrative.

s5.line: £2,707 walks back down the claims to contributors
s5.para: Most of the £2,707 comes from the town, £2,408, with £291 from institutions and the agent. Sixty per cent goes to the Courier, twenty per cent as the reporter's commission (£541), ten to infrastructure and ten to evidence contributors: Priya £203, the cycle club £68. Interviewees and anonymous sources are not paid.

s6.line: Break-even comes on day twenty-five; earnings continue for years
s6.para: Version 0.2 adds costs: £1,350 fixed, variable costs 9.3% of revenue. The story breaks even on 5 November. Over two years it earns £4,378, 96% after reopening from institutions and agents. Twelve stories earn £26,523, the reporter £65 an hour. Payments guide investigation, a trust record builds, and the API answers in 583 tokens.

s7.line: Version 0.3 adds a professional finish and safer code
s7.para: Version 0.3 reorganises navigation into five groups with four themes from secrets.sgit.ai. Architect and developer agents applied escaping templates, visible load failures, keyboard focus, chart text summaries and a 44-check gate. The model now has the reporter on payroll with commission, sized by first-week payments, and records editors' expectations against what the town paid.

s8.line: A way to see the argument whole, not forecast
s8.para: The simulation draws in the usually invisible parts: the reporter's work, readers' graphs, buyers beyond the town, agents and the money returning. In one closure journalism helps plan a school run, keep a café open, price a job, inspect eight bridges and route 140 vans. Everything is fictional; Markus Franz's terms are credited to him.
